claim: The CAS merge-layout preparation left open decision D3 unresolved: whether the extracted units should live in new sub-directories (for example `Gc/Round/`, `Pool/Ref/`) or keep the current flat per-layer layout with more files.
P3 was a recurring `stageManifest: manifest ordinal collision`; one instance escaped retry to a foreground query as `LOGICAL_ERROR` 28 seconds after ch1 was mount-fenced.

A content-static ref-shard can permanently orphan a manifest when an abandoned precommit remains in its journal: token-diff `Skip` prevents `reclaimAbandonedPrecommit` from running after the watermark later proves the precommit dead.

republishRef can reach the overwrite leak when a crash or exception occurs after promote(dst) and before dropRef(src), because its source-only idempotency gate then re-stages a fresh ManifestId on retry.

An uncaught `CORRUPTED_DATA` exception from `resolveByExactGet` or `putIfAbsentControlled` in `flushRefBatch` can leave `rt->leader_active` set and `rt->cv` unnotified, wedging the namespace's ref mutation path until restart.

Using raw `tail_since_snapshot.size() > 64` for `maybeScheduleSnapshotPublish` causes continuous snapshot publishing under sustained load because the 5-second grace window alone leaves roughly 115–230 young entries in the tail at combined append rates of 23–46 entries per second.

`trySnapshotPublishOnce` copied the full `RefTableState` once per aged tail entry at `CasStore.cpp:1985`, and the replay-plus-copy loop held `rt->state_mutex`, blocking concurrent `flushRefBatch` admissions for its duration.

A late predecessor log cannot enter the live ref state because `applyRefLogTxn` requires a strict increase over `greatest_applied`; it also does not enter `tail_since_snapshot` without a steady-state re-list, so it is visible only to cold folds during a race-dependent divergent-observer window before a covering snapshot and then becomes permanently invisible.

`WriterPublishSnapshot` must use `CoveredFold`, which excludes `droppedEver` under `Rev6MountRule`; otherwise a later snapshot can silently re-include a dropped id and make `INV_SNAP_DETERMINISTIC` unsatisfiable.
Without a `MOVING_DIR_NAME` parser case, every file under `<table>/moving/<part>/` routes to the literal ref `moving`, causing all files and all moved parts to collide.

Before the incremental-budget change, `admits()` fully rebuilt and encoded both a snapshot and a hypothetical whole-namespace removal transaction for every state-growing operation, making a K-op batch against N live refs cost O(K×N).

`RefCowMap::find` creates a non-mergeable base iterator for an overlay-only key, so incrementing the iterator can skip later base entries even though the primitive is documented as a `std::map` replacement.

`RefTableState` has accumulated keyed lookup, ordered canonical scans, cheap snapshots, batch apply, incremental byte accounting, manifest-owner uniqueness, and mass replay while remaining a mutable struct whose derived fields can be bypassed by direct mutation.

Using `std::unordered_map` for the `RefCowManifestSet` overlay increased scratch-copy cost by 37% to 42% because copying an empty unordered map allocates a bucket array; the overlay was changed to `std::map`.

Snapshot publication must re-evaluate the accumulated tail or remember and re-fire a pending trigger, because single-flight suppression can otherwise let a publication of chunk 1 hide chunks 2 through N indefinitely.

A ref-log transaction can become durable before its in-memory apply throws, allowing a later transaction to apply without contiguity checking and a snapshot to label the state with the later transaction id, permanently hiding the earlier transaction from recovery.

The stage-1 ref-lane leader originally published `leader_active = true` before allocating its first responsibility entry, so an allocation exception could strand the leadership baton and block later appends indefinitely.

A publish appends both `precommitAdd` and `promote` ref-log transactions; `precommitAdd` carries the activation `+1` edge, while `promote` moves the owner at the same `manifest_ref` and emits no edge.
Because read-created catalog entries are not reclaimed, reads against nonexistent tables can grow the one pool-wide catalog without bound and exhaust admission capacity for legitimate creations.
A permanent `Retired` catalog history grows with every historical namespace and eventually makes legitimate admissions return `LIMIT_EXCEEDED`; normal `Atomic` UUID churn does not bound that history.

An immortal `Retired` row makes the catalog `O(historical namespaces)` on the hot full-object CAS path and eventually exhausts the catalog's admission budget; exact compaction is unavailable for arbitrary opaque names.
Namespace removal can miss a build between allocation and registration, allowing a paused build to publish `NamespaceBirth` after cancellation and resurrect the removed namespace.
Concurrent verbatim append can lose updates because CAS retry reuses stale `old + suffix` data instead of rereading the winner's value; the path is used for mutation-entry CSN append.

`Pool::beginPartWrite` has an allocate/register window in which a build can be allocated after a drop sweep snapshots `inflight_builds`, reviving an empty ownerless `Live` namespace that GC does not sweep.
A damaged `_ckpt` is isolated to a per-namespace hold, but that hold still shuts the round-wide destructive gate and `publishCkpt` has no repair path because it hits the same decode failure.

The catalog's single-object atomicity makes every table creation contend on the same CAS target, turning high-rate table creation into timeout-prone serialization; reverting to unreliable pool LIST is not the accepted fix direction.

Before its fix, `Build::promote` could overwrite an existing committed `refs[R]` without emitting a removal for the old binding, leaving two committed owner bindings for `R` and permanently pinning the old manifest and uniquely-owned blobs.

Treating a vanished catalog as an empty catalog is unsafe: the retry path could replace every namespace's catalog with a single mutation's output via create-if-absent; `PoolMeta::admitOrValidate` is the fail-closed analogue.
The strict sequence-1 grammar requiring prev_epoch_seal on every non-genesis epoch is unusable because the ordinary {E,1} append path does not copy the recovered predecessor seal
The Stage A plan omits CasRefLedger::trySnapshotPublishOnce as a writer of checkpoint_snapshot_id, so the checkpoint witness and cleanup authority are absent from the claimed INV-4 implementation

The per-namespace life_epoch design is not executable because the plan retains validateEpochSealGrammar(const RefLogTxn &) and does not propagate life_epoch through encodeRefLogTxn, decodeRefLogTxn, and their callers
The plan still prescribes the stale validateEpochSealGrammar API in its Grammar paragraph, Step 3, and Task 6 Consumes block despite intending a structural/contextual split
Recovery can publish seal S without advancing result.state.greatest_applied to S, so the next epoch's first log uses prev=A instead of prev=S and GC can accept a late void log below the cursor
Using {0,0} as a rebirth anchor after retiring a namespace cursor destroys durable lineage: an old log can be folded twice, while preserving prev=R can leave a missing retired anchor
An empty unclean recovery publishes no seal, so a genuinely void first record has no durable certificate and can be folded as writer-unapplied data or skipped without proof

A chain-repair 404 can be legitimate after concurrent snapshot publication and deletion, so recovery must route it through a bounded vanish-restart loop rather than classify it immediately as corruption
Recovery repair buffering can exhaust memory because the plan collects an entire omitted run even though transactions can be 20 MiB and current recovery retains only one decoded transaction
Voidness cannot be inferred from recovery's {my_epoch - 1, UINT64_MAX} seal because burned mount epochs can make the seal's epoch differ from the actual dead writer epoch

Allowing sealed_from={0,0} does not encode a never-born namespace because Removed without remove_txn_id is rejected by the snapshot codec; an explicit NeverBorn state or separate seal format is required
Vanish-restart can discard chain evidence and later succeed from an older snapshot when a second lying LIST omits both the selected successor and its missing predecessor
A latest-pointer-only _seal_latest forgets earlier unconsumed void intervals, so a ghost in an earlier interval can be folded after a later seal overwrites the pointer
A later first recovery pointer can invalidate a valid clean genesis record with prev=0, and a lineage-only pointer state for removal before any seal is not defined

Recovery cannot safely identify a namespace snapshot base from LIST when covered logs may have been deleted; it needs a point-readable authority containing at least the namespace incarnation, authoritative checkpoint ID, and last epoch seal.
Deleting a snapshot candidate before its _ckpt pointer CAS can leave _ckpt pointing to a missing object because backend CAS checks the expected pointer token but not target existence.
Strict ref-key parsing that accepts only _log, _snap, and _cleanup will abort a fold round when _ckpt appears under cas/refs/<ns>/.
`CasRefCatalog` has no entry-deletion API in the documented state, so a catalog entry survives unconditionally rather than through a partially completed multi-step removal path.
The fence-race `/Replacement` fixture's successor `_ckpt` is life-scoped: the predecessor `_ckpt` at incarnation 177 cannot satisfy a successor at incarnation 178.

An uncaught `CORRUPTED_DATA` from `resolveByExactGet` or `putIfAbsentControlled` in `flushRefBatch` can leave `leader_active` set and waiters blocked indefinitely; the remaining queue must be completed with the exception and notified.
`Build::promote` overwrites `refs[R]` without emitting a committed-to-committed repoint event, so the previously committed manifest and its uniquely owned blobs remain pinned forever.
A crash or exception after `republishRef` promotes the destination ref but before it drops the source ref causes a retry to mint a fresh manifest and leak the first committed destination manifest.
After a lost-ACK `dropRef` CAS, replaying the closure can throw `FILE_DOESNT_EXIST` even though the ref removal already committed; conditional-write conflicts should reconcile the post-state instead.
A lost-ACK publish or promote can replay its closure and append a duplicate journal event, producing journal bloat even though set-based GC keeps blob in-degree semantically correct.

E5's in-place-materialize fast path was unreachable from production: `flushRefBatch`'s trial-validation copy `working` stayed alive to function scope, pinning a second shared_ptr reference to the live base across the post-PUT install so `materializeCommitted()` always saw `use_count()==2` and took the O(N) copy path; fixed by releasing `working` before id allocation so the live base is uniquely owned at the install point.

A race existed where the relaxed `use_count()` load in the in-place-materialize fast path could race a cross-thread shared_ptr release: `trySnapshotPublishOnce`'s `candidate_state` (a shared-base copy) was destroyed at function return outside the lock. Fixed by resetting `candidate_state` under `state_mutex` immediately after `snapshotOf`, covering every exit path.

A retry path that treats a vanished CAS catalog object as an empty catalog is a silent-default-substitution defect: on retry after a vanish, it would replace every namespace's catalog with a single mutation's output via create-if-absent; the in-tree analogue `PoolMeta::admitOrValidate` already fails closed on exactly that observation and was cited as the pattern to follow.

`Build::promote` can overwrite an existing committed ref (`refs[dst]=T_a`) with a new manifest (`T_b`) without releasing `T_a`, permanently orphaning (leaking) the old manifest and its blobs; this is the most concrete confirmed storage leak from the review. Fix: `Build::promote` must, when `refs[R]` already names another manifest, either emit a proper committed-to-committed repoint or fail closed with an exception; also move `Build::abandon`'s `retireBuildSeq` call after the removal mutation.

Risk register #5 (Medium, confirmed): `moveDirectory`'s RENAME TABLE path (`:980-1006`) is non-atomic across namespaces; a mid-loop throw can leave the table split across two namespaces (documented as re-drivable), producing an operator-visible split state until manual re-drive. Suggested action: track as a known limitation, consider a durable move journal pre-release.

`RefCowMap::find` builds a non-mergeable iterator for overlay-only keys by using `base->find(key)` instead of the sibling base branch's `lower_bound`; with base={A,D} and overlay-only B, `find("B")` then `++` hits a state bitwise equal to `end()` and silently skips D. Not reachable through current point-dereference-only callers, but the fix (`lower_bound`) is a strict improvement, identical when the key is shadowed.
Per-table refs use an append-only log plus periodic snapshot, and CasRefStateMachine computes RefTableState = replay(snapshot, tail) for writers, recovery, GC intake, and fsck.
The all-tree part-files design stores txn_version.txt, metadata_version.txt, and uuid.txt as ordinary entries in the part manifest rather than a separate ref sidecar.
`mutable_files` such as `txn_version.txt` are inlined into the root shard's `RootRef` protobuf and add zero S3 operations.
After the all-tree part-files migration, `uuid.txt`, `txn_version.txt`, and `metadata_version.txt` are ordinary manifest entries and no longer populate `RootRef.mutable_files`.
`FREEZE` creates per-part shadow refs under `shadow/<name>/…`; unchanged parts share blobs by hash and the refs act as GC reachability roots.
A fresh pool mints its own owner and epoch, while imported manifests cannot collide with new ones because `ManifestId` includes the namespace.
The only mutable CAS data is ref state binding a part name to a manifest id; blobs, part manifests, and their metadata are write-once objects.
A precommit may name only a manifest minted by the transaction or the ref's current committed manifest; granting fresh ownership to a foreign manifest id is rejected to prevent ABA reuse.
Publishing over an existing ref binding throws; an intentional repoint must use `republishRef`.
The append-mode `writeFile` path is safe only under the single-appender invariant: it freezes the carried prefix when opened and its CAS loop re-reads the token but not the base content.
A `ManifestRef` has at most one owner in a table, in either the `Committed` or `Precommit` slot.
The former `RefSidecar` and mutable-per-part-file classification are deleted; `uuid.txt`, `txn_version.txt`, and `metadata_version.txt` are ordinary manifest entries.
A part manifest contains `ref`, `root_namespace_id`, `payload_digest`, and strictly path-sorted `entries`; `payload_digest` is integrity/debug metadata rather than a key or GC edge.
A manifest id is `ManifestRef = {writer_epoch, build_sequence, manifest_ordinal}` and is not a content hash or random value.
Ref transaction ids are per-namespace contiguous pairs `(writer_epoch, ref_sequence)` rendered as fixed-width hexadecimal fields; `applyRefLogTxn` rejects a non-successor id with `CORRUPTED_DATA`.
The ref lane has no append-to-object or CAS-swapped mutable pointer: ref logs and snapshots are immutable objects created with conditional creates, and only GC deletes ref objects.
Under D1, `listNamespaces` is derived from a LIST of `cas/refs/` and is unioned with `roots/` for namespaces containing only verbatim files.

Rebuild edge reconstruction replays committed owner state and live precommit bindings, validates every committed `PartManifest` with `refMatchesBody` and `manifestNamespaceMatches`, and refuses the whole rebuild on a missing or invalid committed manifest body.

The queue leader increments `root.shard_version` after every closure in queue order rather than once per flush, so each promise receives its own post-bump transition version and one `casPut` may carry multiple ordered events.
A create-if-absent mutation with `token == nullopt` flushes alone using its `birth_incarnation` and `birth_floor_provider`, preserving the existing birth-stamping behavior.
The new `ShardCoverage` fields are `has_live_precommit`, `min_live_precommit_writer_epoch`, and `min_live_precommit_build_sequence`, and they round-trip through the fold-seal codec.

`ShardCoverage` stores the lexicographically minimal `{writer_epoch, build_sequence}` among live precommit bindings, stamps it on every Read visit, and carries it through Skip and durable fold-seal restart.
`ManifestPut` records `object_kind = Manifest`, the owning namespace, `manifestRefDebugString(id.ref)`, the body token, and reason `stageManifest: part-manifest body written`.

`PrecommitRemoved` records `object_kind = Root`, the target namespace and ref, `manifestRefDebugString(precommit_manifest)`, and reason `abandon: precommit binding removed`; GC-side removals remain `PrecommitReclaim` events.
Decoded `PartManifest::entries` must be strictly ascending by `path`; binary search and all index-free folder-view queries rely on this invariant.

`Store::readManifestShared` has the same mandatory `HEAD`, fail-closed `FILE_DOESNT_EXIST` and `CORRUPTED_DATA` behavior, and manifest-cache insertion semantics as `readManifest`, but returns the cached `std::shared_ptr<const PartManifest>` without a per-call copy.
`resolveRef(allow_stale=true)` is bounded by `shard_decode_cache_ttl_ms` and locally write-coherent because committed shard mutations erase the shard decode-cache entry and bump `shard_write_seq`.
`decodePartManifest` rejects `path <= prev_path`; the encoder already emits sorted entries, and the strict ordering guarantee is what makes `PartFolderView` index-free.

The byte-weighted manifest decode cache remains keyed by `(ManifestId, Token)`; a token mismatch causes a fresh `GET` and decode, a failed decode is not cached, and the mandatory manifest `HEAD` remains.
A same-manifest re-promote is allowed and must be idempotent; the guard compares the existing manifest_ref with the manifest_ref being promoted rather than rejecting every already-committed ref.
republishRef compares only the source and destination PartManifest entries and drops the source ref without staging a new manifest when the entries match.
Build::promote proceeds when the target ref is absent or already names the same manifest_ref, and throws ABORTED when it names a different committed manifest_ref.
republishRef determines idempotency from PartManifest::entries, not ManifestId, because a re-drive mints a new manifest ID for the same content.
PartManifest::entries are canonical path-sorted vectors, so element-wise vector equality is stable for comparing source and destination content.
When the destination ref is absent, republishRef retains the normal stageManifest → precommitAdd → promote → dropRef sequence.

The obsolete ref handoff transfers a contiguous writer-log prefix into the GC generation through the existing single `gc/state` CAS; before that CAS the prefix is authoritative, and after it the GC fold is authoritative.

`dropNamespace` is represented as one constant-size `remove_namespace` transaction that atomically clears committed and precommit bindings and changes the incarnation to `Removed`; it does not serialize the owner list.
A writer-log object can be removed only when the adopted fold seal names a valid `RefBaseSet` whose namespace row has the same incarnation and `folded_seq >= log_record.seq`.
Every writer-log key and GC ref-fold entry contains the namespace incarnation, so an older incarnation cannot cover or consume a newer incarnation's sequence numbers.
`remove_namespace` changes `Live` to `Removed` and clears every owner binding in one replay transition; no later mutation is valid for that incarnation.

A warm-cache isolated ref mutation creates one `_log` object and performs zero ref-state reads, while a compatible batch of `B` mutations shares one `putIfAbsent`; uncertain writes are resolved by an exact-key `GET`.
The same `WriterId` identifies build ownership, the prefix of each `ManifestRef`, and a namespace incarnation; `birth_gc_round` remains separate and orders a new namespace incarnation relative to GC.
`ManifestRef` is `{writer_id, manifest_ordinal}` with ordinal range 1 through 999999, and canonical manifest paths include `cas/manifests/<namespace>/<writer_id>/<000001>.proto`.
All archive namespaces end in `@cas@`, and `shadowNamespace` must preserve that suffix.

A `RefLogTxn` contains `header`, `namespace`, `namespace_incarnation`, `seq`, and repeated `RefOp ops`; supported operations are `namespace_birth`, `owner_transition`, `set_payload`, `clear_precommits_before`, and `remove_namespace`.

A transaction containing `namespace_birth` and its optional first owner transition runs alone; `clear_precommits_before` and `remove_namespace` also run alone, and a batch never crosses its encoded-size or operation-count limit.

`namespace_birth` is operation zero of sequence one, creates `Live` state for the physical incarnation key, normally includes the first precommit add, and has `birth_gc_round` no greater than the current decoded `gc/state.round`.
A promote operation requires `Live` state, the exact old precommit, a committed binding naming the same `ManifestRef`, and a complete initial `RootRef` payload.
A committed ref removal requires the exact committed binding and removes its `RootRef` payload.
A payload update requires a live committed ref still naming `expected_manifest_ref`; it replaces the complete mutable payload and changes no reachability edge.

Applying `remove_namespace` clears committed refs, precommits, and payloads, changes state to `Removed`, and makes a second durable remove record corruption; API idempotency returns success after observing `Removed`.
A successful append leaves no dirty ref-state memory because the log is authoritative; complete namespace views may be evicted immediately, and eviction never writes storage.

The common write path validates under the namespace lock, writes one inline key or deterministic batch transaction with `putIfAbsent`, resolves an uncertain precondition failure by reading the same key, and applies the transition to memory only after the log is authoritative.
A namespace recreation at the same archive path is allowed only after the old namespace-file prefix is empty, uses a strictly greater `NamespaceIncarnation`, and starts again at sequence one.

Ref-base row keys are `NamespaceMeta`, `Committed`, or `Precommit` tuples beginning with `LogPrefix(ns) = canonical_namespace_bytes(ns) || "/_log/"`; memcomparable encoding preserves canonical object-key `LIST` order, including prefix-related namespaces.

GC processes namespaces in canonical tuple-key order, selects at most one complete transaction prefix per namespace per generation, and never returns to a namespace after emitting its output; any suffix remains in `_log` for a later generation.

A writer mutation exists exactly when a durable operation exists in its `_log` object; one `_log` object may contain a bounded flat-combined batch, and its key plus body are the complete operation encoding.
Only the mounted writer allocates namespace log sequence numbers; GC never appends to the writer log.
Every owner add, move, payload update, removal, and namespace removal is a writer-log operation; GC only replays those operations.
The existing GC generation CAS co-adopts reachability runs, the fold seal, and the exact `RefBaseSet`; there is no independent ref adoption state.
An append that exceeds the namespace tail or decoded-row bound fails before object creation and retains the current sequence.
Mixed manifests store one `BlobRef ref` per `ManifestEntry`; the entry payload is `placement u8, algo u8, digest <lenFor(algo)> raw BE bytes, blob_size u64, inline_len u32, inline`.
The per-manifest `blob_hash_len` header is removed in mixed-algorithm pools, and an unknown entry algorithm fails decoding with `CORRUPTED_DATA`.

For a table snapshot `S_X`, recovery computes `TableState = Replay(S_X.state, tail(X))`, where `tail(X)` contains every valid log transaction with identifier greater than `X`; without a snapshot, recovery starts from the empty state and `namespace_birth`.
A snapshot reuses the `RefTxnId` of its last included log, producing one shared ordered timeline where `log X == snapshot X` and later logs have greater identifiers.
`RefTxnId` is distinct from `build_sequence` and `build_id`; a build may create multiple ref transactions and transactions may contain operations from multiple builds.
A `Removed` snapshot contains no committed refs or precommits, and a later `namespace_birth` with a greater `RefTxnId` recreates the namespace on the same timeline.
Promotion removes an exact precommit and creates the committed binding to the same manifest in one transaction, installing the complete initial mutable payload without an ownerless interval.
`remove_namespace` is the final operation in its transaction, follows exact owner transitions for every committed ref and precommit, requires empty owner sets, and records its own `remove_txn_id`.
At most one ref-log PUT per table may have an unresolved result; a later same-table PUT cannot start until the earlier result is resolved.
Warm table mutations perform no ref `LIST`, snapshot GET, `gc/state` read, HEAD, or compare-and-swap; they append one deterministic log object and update cached state.
Failed precommit cleanup is persisted by the writer before build retirement; GC does not detect or remove dead precommits by itself.

Owner transitions emit direct manifest-edge events: owner addition is `+1`, removal is `-1`, same-manifest promotion is neutral, replacement emits old `-1` and new `+1`, and mutable-payload updates emit no edge.

The ref protocol stores per-table append-only `_log/<txn-id>` objects and writer-published `_snap/<id>.proto` snapshots; `GC` folds per-table cursors and manifest-edge deltas from one global `LIST`, cleans covered objects, and never reconstructs table state.

Ref transaction IDs contain nonzero `writer_epoch` and `ref_sequence`; `renderRefTxnId` renders canonical IDs as `0000000000000007-000000000000008e`, and `parseRefTxnId` accepts only the canonical form.
Ref log operations are exactly `NamespaceBirth`, `OwnerTransition`, `SetPayload`, and `RemoveNamespace`; owner bindings distinguish `Committed` and `Precommit` owners.
Ref table snapshots have `Live` or `Removed` lifecycle, optional `remove_txn_id`, committed rows sorted by `ref_name`, and precommits sorted by `(ref_name, mref)`.
Ref snapshot encoding requires committed and precommit inputs to be sorted and rejects unsorted or duplicate rows; a `Removed` snapshot must have zero rows and a `remove_txn_id`.

A ref append lane obtains `ref_sequence` from a store-wide counter, permits at most one unresolved PUT per table, blocks that table's lane while unresolved, and applies observed durable state to the cache before unwedging.

The ref batching queue creates one compatible `RefLogTxn`, validates requests with per-request undo against cached state, gives invalid requests their own exceptions, runs birth and removal alone, and limits each batch to one operation per ref name.

Snapshot publication is background and off-lane, uses `snapshot_log_count_threshold`, `snapshot_log_bytes_threshold`, mount-time triggers, and `snapshot_min_log_age_ms`, and resolves uncertain publication by exact-key byte comparison.

`dropNamespace` emits one transaction naming every owner followed by `remove_namespace`, applies it in memory, rejects further operations, and publishes a constant-size `Removed` snapshot after durability.
Recreating a removed namespace requires the exact `_cleanup` marker found during recovery and continues the existing transaction-ID timeline.

When `flushRefBatch` catches a `CORRUPTED_DATA` exception, it must complete pending and carved survivor requests with that exception, reset `rt->leader_active`, notify `rt->cv`, keep the wedge on corruption, and rethrow.

The ref-model rev.6 oracle is `WStateRev6 == FoldIds(EmptyState, writtenEver \ droppedEver)`, and the strict `NoDivergentFold` invariant requires every completed reader under `Rev6MountRule` to reconstruct that oracle.
The rev.6 snapshot codec stores optional `RefTableSnapshot::sealed_from`, uses format version 2, rejects version 1 fail-closed, and throws when `sealed_from` is greater than `snapshot_id`.

On an unclean epoch boundary, recovery publishes a seal with `seal_id = RefTxnId{liveWriterEpoch() - 1, UINT64_MAX}`, `snapshot_id = seal_id`, and `sealed_from = greatest listed txn id` before marking the ref table recovered; a failed seal PUT throws and leaves recovery fail-closed.

The recovery seal is skipped when the boundary is clean, the live writer epoch is below 2, the dead-epoch region is empty, the table is already sealed through the boundary, or the recovered lifecycle is not `Live`.

The publish trigger uses `tail_count_since_snapshot` or `tail_bytes_since_snapshot` above configured thresholds and no longer requires entries to age; `snapshot_min_log_age_ms`, `TailLogEntry`, `tail_since_snapshot`, `snapshot_base_state`, and `CasRefLatePredecessorObserved` are removed.

A late `_log` with id `L` satisfying `sealed_from < L <= newest_snapshot_id` is reported with a warning and one `RefLateLogDetected` event, never GET-revived, and left for ordinary covered-log cleanup.
At an unclean mount, recovery LIST and replay are followed by an immediate snapshot PUT seal before the mount opens writable.
The recovery seal ID is `RefTxnId(my_epoch - 1, 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF)`, which covers every late log from every dead epoch below `my_epoch`.

Snapshot publication copies the live state once at a transaction boundary when the count threshold exceeds `snapshot_log_count_threshold` or the bytes threshold fires, then encodes and PUTs asynchronously.
A lane refuses to allocate new IDs past an unresolved PUT in release builds and uses `chassert` for the same wedge invariant in debug builds.
A standalone committed-file removal without a directory drop publishes one repoint containing the manifest without the removed entry.
A repoint publishes the new manifest closure before backend observation and atomically moves ownership onto the same ref key; the old manifest is reclaimed by normal GC.
A byte-equal repoint is a zero-mutation no-op with no audit event.
The repoint primitive serializes concurrent repoints through the per-table single-writer ref lane and promote CAS.
For a ref key `K`, `repointRef` maps to `WRepoint(mOld, mNew, ref=K, w)`: one journal event in one namespace carries `old=Bind(mOld)` and `new=Bind(mNew)` under the same ref.

`Build::promote` accepts a trailing `bool allow_repoint = false`; when it is true and the committed ref names a different manifest, it emits one committed-transition RefOp from the current `ManifestRef` to the new `id.ref` and emits `CasEventType::RefRepoint`.

`repointRef(const PartRefKey &, std::vector<Cas::ManifestEntry>, Cas::ProvenanceOp)` returns false and performs zero pool mutations or events when the candidate manifest is byte-equal to the committed manifest; otherwise it publishes with `allow_repoint=true`, increments `ProfileEvents::CasRefRepoint`, logs the ref and entry count at warning level, and erases the cached folder view on success.

After the mutable-file deletion sweep, resolved refs contain `manifest_id`, `manifest_size`, and `published_at_ms`, while the access API is `publishEntries(dst, entries, op, allow_repoint)` and no production code retains mutable-file fields or predicates.
The CAS refsnaplog migration covers `cas_ref_log` objects at `_log/<txn_id>` and `cas_ref_snap` objects at `_snap/<snapshot_id>`, moving both from binary codecs to the phase-1 text file shape.
A `cas_ref_log` object represents exactly one committed `RefLogTxn`, containing one namespace, one transaction ID, and that transaction's vector of `RefOp` entries.
The recovery seal is an ordinary `RefTableSnapshot` published at synthetic `snapshot_id = {my_epoch-1, UINT64_MAX}` with `sealed_from` set to the greatest applied reference transaction ID.
`sealed_from` is an optional `RefTxnId` whose absence and presence must remain distinguishable in the snapshot wire format; it is not represented by a sentinel value.
Every `RefTxnId` field in refsnaplog text, including the synthetic seal sequence `UINT64_MAX`, is serialized as a decimal string rather than a JSON number.
Snapshot committed rows are strictly ascending by `ref_name`, precommits are strictly ascending by `(ref_name, manifest_ref)`, and every precommit has `kind == Precommit`.

The CAS manifest and `checksums.txt` must be built from the transaction-visible state, including staged projection files, or the published part can diverge from the files intended by the writer.
`MergeTreeData::removePartsInRangeFromWorkingSet` explicitly commits the CA transaction before the in-memory rollback so an empty covering part publishes its ref before the rollback.
The `commit`-implies-`precommit` guard emits the `CasImplicitPrecommitInCommit` ProfileEvent and a debug log when commit performs the implicit precommit.

A RefShard's journal is an append-only log of +/- ownership events retained until GC trim (gated by gc_trim_min_events / gc_trim_body_soft_limit settings) advances past the sealed fold cursor covering them (INV-JOURNAL-COVERAGE); the incarnation field is a durable strictly monotone (writer_epoch, build_sequence) pair stamped at (re)creation and never changed, closing the ABA hazard for a fold cursor keyed by (ns, shard, incarnation).

A PartManifest records (file_name -> blob_hash, size, placement) for every content-addressed file; EntryPlacement has Inline (tiny files embedded in the manifest body, part-open cost = 1 GET) and Blob (large standalone file at blobs/<H>); a third placement kind, pack_slice (member of a pack object at (pack_hash, abs_offset, length)), is a reserved design idea with no EntryPlacement enum value in the code.

PartManifest bodies live at cas/manifests/<ns>/<writer_epoch>/<build_sequence>/<ordinal>.proto with a 6-digit zero-padded ordinal filename; a manifest's identity (ManifestId) is a root_namespace paired with a nested ManifestRef of (writer_epoch, build_sequence, manifest_ordinal), not a type literally named PartManifestId, and is unique by construction since every component is durable-monotone and never reused.

The residual Late-Predecessor-PUT ref-loss race is mitigated only by the snapshot_min_log_age_ms grace window (a candidate ref snapshot never covers a tail region younger than this age); ProfileEvents::CasRefLatePredecessorObserved increments once per trySnapshotPublishOnce call in which that grace window forces an early break, making the residual race measurable rather than only mitigated.

Every cross-thread copy of a live `RefTableState` must be created AND destroyed under `state_mutex`, so that a `use_count()` of 1 observed under that lock is stable against both increment and decrement; this invariant is documented in both COW headers (`RefCowMap`, `RefCowManifestSet`).

The in-place fold's coherence ordering: per overlay entry, the base mutation (its only throw point) runs first, then the non-throwing `net_delta` adjust and `overlay.erase`; at every escape point `(base, overlay, net_delta)` stays exactly coherent, load-bearing because materialize runs after a durable PUT and a tracked-allocator OOM must not corrupt live bookkeeping.

In-place trusted-replay apply is safe because every production call site of `admits`/`applyRefLogTxn`/`replay` runs either under the ledger's `state_mutex` or on a detached/local copy, so no concurrent reader can observe a state mid-mutation; COW writes touch only the per-copy overlay, never the shared immutable base.

The recovery-latency fix (G) materializes only the one retained recovery-adopt site (`CasRefLedger.cpp:426`) before retaining its replayed state; the fsck/GC `replay`/`recoverRefTable` locals (`CasFsck.cpp`, `CasOrphanManifestSweep.cpp`, `CasGc.cpp`) are iterated once and dropped, so they are deliberately left unmaterialized.

The flat-combining shard-mutation queue (`Store::mutateShard`) serializes intra-server writers per `(namespace, shard)`: the caller finding the queue leaderless flushes batches (one read, apply-all in order with per-closure snapshot isolation, one `casPut`) until its own item completes; the carve runs after the flush's first read so S3 read latency IS the batching window, turning the old positive-feedback conflict loop under load into a negative one. At most one mutation per ref name is allowed per flush; `WholeShard` closures (trim, fence, dropNamespace, reclaim) and create-if-absent flushes run solo.

The ref-lane flush uses a per-table "wedge": at most one outstanding record per table holding the key and sealed bytes of a single conditional PUT whose outcome is unresolved. The next flush must resolve that exact key (via `resolveByExactGet`) before it may allocate a new transaction id, which is what realizes INV-14 (fail-closed on ambiguity) and prevents the ledger from ever silently creating a gap or double-publishing.

`RefTableState` holds a copy-on-write map of committed rows, a set of precommits, an O(1) manifest-ownership index enforcing the one-owner-per-manifest invariant, a lifecycle (`Live`/`Removed`), the greatest applied transaction id, and O(1)-maintained body-size counters for admission. Two mutexes have a fixed lock order `ref_queue_mutex -> state_mutex`, never the reverse, and network I/O is never performed under `state_mutex`, so a reader sees either a whole transaction or none of it.

Recovery of a ref table on first touch performs a paginated LIST of `cas/ns/stream/<life-id>/`, takes the greatest snapshot, replays every log strictly greater than it one transaction at a time, restarts on a vanished object (bounded at 3 attempts, treated as concurrent GC cleanup rather than corruption), and on an unclean boundary publishes a recovery seal snapshot at the synthetic id `{my_epoch - 1, UINT64_MAX}` before exposing the table, so that id dominates any straggler the dead epoch could still materialize.

Under CAS's `RefLaneState` model, relink certification is Ready-state-only: a resumed relink gate consumes a single-state precondition instead of the twelve-row cross-product the earlier encoding required, and the NETWORK_ERROR/terminal split means only `Closed`/`Faulted` are non-retriable while all other states retry.

The ref state machine's load-bearing invariant is that `promote` never silently displaces a different committed row for the same name; a silent displacement would never emit the evicted manifest's -1 edge, leaking it phantom-alive forever. `stateFromSnapshot` round-trips a hand-built snapshot through the codec so the same bug class cannot enter via snapshot loading.

`cleanupRefObjects` only deletes ref logs/snapshots that are covered by BOTH the durable fold cursor AND a durable snapshot; GC never invents a ref transition, and dead-precommit cleanup (appending exact owner_transition removals) is the writer's job, not GC's.

Ref transaction IDs (`RefTxnId = {writer_epoch, ref_sequence}`) are strictly increasing with epoch as the primary component, so a recreated namespace always gets greater ids than a prior life — no ABA check is needed on ref-log ordering.

Loose mountpoint files are not namespaces — they are path-owned plain objects with conditional overwrite/exact deletion, drained by server-root decommission. Directory creation has no durable representation and creates no catalog row. Detached and moving parts are ref-name prefixes inside the owning table's namespace, not separate namespaces.

CA namespace mapping: a detached part uses the same table namespace with ref `detached/<part>` (no parallel namespace, B181 fold); a FREEZE shadow uses the literal shadow table directory as namespace (bijective, pool-global); verbatim table-level files (`format_version.txt`, `deduplication_logs/…`, mutation entries) are namespace files; loose startup-probe files are plain mountpoint objects at `roots/<server_root_id>/<path>`.

Mutable per-part files (`kMutablePerPartFiles`: `uuid.txt`, `txn_version.txt`, `metadata_version.txt`, plus `.tmp` siblings) live in `RefPayload.mutable_files`, never in the shared manifest tree, and are matched on the last path component only.

`CasManifestCodec` (`CAPT` magic) encodes `format_version`, `writer_version`, `ref{epoch,seq,ordinal}`, the namespace, a `payload_digest` (integrity/debug only, never a key/dedup/in-degree input), and entries as an embedded RunFile keyed by path; the decoder enforces strict ascending canonical path order and rejects duplicate paths, an invariant `findEntry`/`entryRange` binary search relies on.
Projection files are nested keys in the parent part's single manifest at paths such as <proj>.proj/<file>, rather than separate refs or sub-manifests.
The mutable per-(namespace, shard) root-shard manifest was removed by `318291fe5e5` and replaced with `CasRefSnapshotCodec`, `CasRefLogCodec`, and `CasRefIntake`.
`Store::mutateShard` groups mutations for one `(namespace, shard)` into one read and one `casPut` per flush.
A CAS snapshot copies the table's current `_snap` body into `cas/refs/shadow/<name>/<table>@cas@/_snap/<txn>.proto` and adds one metadata object, while reusing the referenced part manifests.
A byte-equal repoint performs zero pool mutations, including no manifest PUT and no ref-log record.

For trimmed-but-live precommits whose create event was trimmed, the rebuild lists `cas/manifests/` and over-protects manifests that are not committed, not named by a live-precommit binding, and not provably build-dead by `prefixEligible`.
The observability package emits `ManifestPut` after `Build::stageManifest` writes a body and emits `PrecommitRemoved` after `Build::abandon` removes a precommit binding.
`readManifest` remains a by-value compatibility shim over `readManifestShared` for callers that still require a value.
`adoptPartFromManifest` is consolidated onto `publishEntries`; sender identity is non-authoritative, while decoded entries are adopted as tokenless write evidence and re-proved during promotion.

`shard_decode_cache` remains in `Cas::Store` with its TTL, `shard_write_seq`, and single-flight machinery, and `dedup_cache` remains there because neither should move into a new aggregate cache state.
republishRef is idempotent when the destination is already committed with the same content; a different-content destination is an ABORTED conflict.

In the obsolete ref-log design, `cas/refs` is only an append-only inbox from the mounted writer to GC, and authoritative namespace state is the adopted GC ref fold plus the contiguous writer-log tail.
Phase 1 of the obsolete ref-log design rewrites one complete folded ref base for each productive handoff, while idle and deferred rounds carry the exact parent base without reading or rewriting it.
A table's durable ref state is `latest table snapshot + table transaction logs after that snapshot`; snapshots are complete table states and each log object is one atomic writer transaction.
Live snapshots are published only by the writer from its complete cached state; GC never reconstructs table state and may publish only the constant-size `Removed` snapshot for a removed namespace.
Phase 1 replaces mutable `RootShardManifest` ref storage with an immutable snapshot+log protocol.

The wiring tests stop accepting legacy numeric ref-shard keys and classify current ref writes under `/cas/refs/` with `_log/` or `_snap/`; the two disabled tree-model tests remain deliberate documentation.

Publish-from-live copies `rt->state` exactly once under `state_mutex` at a transaction boundary, encodes and conditionally writes outside the lock, and adopts the result by subtracting captured tail counters instead of replaying `snapshot_base_state` plus `tail_since_snapshot`.
The recovery seal is the only snapshot whose ID is an upper bound of a covered region rather than a real transaction ID.
`snapshot_min_log_age_ms`, its age gates, `CasRefLatePredecessorObserved`, and young-entry replay bookkeeping are removed from the ref protocol.
The proposal raised `snapshot_log_count_threshold` from 64 to 256 and replaced grace-window replay with copy-once-from-live publication.
Committed-part standalone add and overwrite operations use an audited manifest repoint rather than failing closed or silently doing nothing.
The writer's snapshot publication policy gains an age trigger so slowly changing tables periodically publish a small snapshot and do not leave readers with an ancient base.
A committed CAS repoint is implemented as the existing `publishEntries` sequence plus an `allow_repoint` mode on `Build::promote`, matching the modeled TLA transition `WRepoint`.

`Pool/CasRefLedger` owns ref-table state and locks, ref transaction allocation and queueing, recovery/seals, snapshot publication, stale-precommit sweeping, cache eviction, remount/shutdown coordination, and ref read/lifecycle entry points.
`CasRefProtocol` contains the ref replay and intake planning logic, while the two ref codecs remain in `Formats/` and are not pulled into the protocol component.

`CasRefLedger` owns the ref-table map, ref-queue and per-table state mutexes, append/recovery/seal lanes, snapshot publication, stale-precommit sweep, cache eviction, remount coordination, and ref lifecycle/read entry points.

The ref-table-copy performance investigation identified three candidate mechanisms for reducing `flushRefBatch` copying from whole-map cost to touched-row cost: a persistent immutable map, an overlay/delta over a shared base, and a copy-on-write wrapper over `std::map`.
The corrected identity design publishes a cloned part under transient ref `moving/<part>` and makes `rename(moving/<part> → <part>)` a committed-ref repoint onto the final ref.

`RefCowMap` consists of an immutable shared `std::shared_ptr<const std::map<String, RefCommittedRow>> base` and a per-copy `std::map<String, std::optional<RefCommittedRow>> overlay`, with present entries as overrides and `nullopt` as tombstones.

Approach A stores `uint64_t snapshot_body_bytes` and `uint64_t removal_body_bytes` on `RefTableState`; the counters exclude header/meta/trailer framing and the removal transaction's terminal `remove_namespace` operation.

The new `admits()` applies the candidate operation to a scratch state and compares `snapshotFramingSize + snapshot_body_bytes` and `removalFramingSize + removal_body_bytes` against the budgets, reducing a flush batch from O(K×N) to O(K) while preserving the existing preview identifiers and framing.

The incremental `admits()` plan replaces the O(N)-per-operation full re-encode with two running body-byte totals on `RefTableState`, turning a K-op flush batch against an N-ref table from O(K×N) into O(K) with byte-identical decisions.

The `admits()` rewrite uses exact framing-size helpers plus the running body counters rather than hand-written delta arithmetic, while preserving the existing `admits` signature and boolean decisions.
`CasRefLedger::ensureRefTableRecovered` retries the whole recovery attempt, including namespace `LIST`, snapshot/log `GET`s, replay, and the seal `PUT`, rather than retrying only the seal.
`hasAnyRefWithPrefix` is intended as an early-exit existence probe that preserves the recovery and stale-precommit maintenance preamble without materializing the full ref map returned by `listRefs`.

The `RefTableState` optimization work requires a closed class whose invariants hold by construction and benchmarks each hot operation before selecting an internal representation by measured performance and code elegance.
The benchmark suite distinguishes `BM_AdmitsAddPrecommit`, which exercises the production `manifestAlreadyOwned` scan, from `BM_Admits`, whose promote shape is O(1) and does not exercise that scan.
Experiment E2 represents manifest ownership with a copy-on-write membership index so uniqueness checks become O(log N) or O(1) without making scratch copies O(N).

Experiment E4 evaluates an immutable shared sorted-vector base with an overlay for `RefCowMap`, preserving its ordered-iteration API while reducing pointer-chasing in merged iteration, snapshot encoding, and materialization.
`RefTableState` was encapsulated as a closed class with private fields and public getters; mutation is restricted to `applyRefLogTxn`, `replay`, `stateFromSnapshot`, and `materializeCommitted`.
Recovery replay streams post-snapshot `RefLogTxn` objects one at a time after sorting keys by transaction ID, reducing recovery memory to O(one transaction) regardless of tail length.

The pre-release CAS policy permits removing `RefOp::payload` and renaming `SetPayload` to `SetPublishedAt` with wire word `set_payload` to `set_published_at` because every existing pool is recreated before release and no old-field decoder tolerance is required.
